summary: ORBITALIS is a web tool that finds moving objects in NASA’s SPHEREx sky-survey data. SPHEREx photographs the same patch of sky on several dates, but no simple tool shows what changed between scans. ORBITALIS pulls real SPHEREx images from the NASA-IPAC archive, removes the static stars, and stacks the scans along about a thousand possible motion paths, so faint movers add up and noise averages away. Users step through the scans, open ranked candidates, and see each one’s track, brightness over time and color spectrum. We test the search by planting fake objects. Every result is a candidate to follow up. It makes real NASA data open to students, volunteers and researchers.
details:
What it does


ORBITALIS is a web tool that finds moving objects in NASA’s SPHEREx data. SPHEREx scans the whole sky again and again, so the same patch of sky is photographed on several dates. A user picks a sky position or a preset field, and ORBITALIS looks for faint things that shift between scans, such as asteroids, comets and distant bodies like a hypothetical Planet X. Users can step through the scans with a time slider, open any candidate, and see how far it moved, how its brightness changed, and a quick-look infrared spectrum across SPHEREx’s colors. Every result is labelled as a candidate.

How it works

  • The backend pulls small calibrated image cutouts from the NASA-IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA).
  • Frames are cleaned, masked and aligned onto one grid, and the static sky (stars and galaxies) is subtracted.
  • We test about 1,000 possible motions. For each one, the frames are shifted along that path and stacked, so a faint mover adds up while random noise averages away.
  • Peaks above 5 times the noise become candidates, ranked by signal strength. We measure brightness along each track.
  • To check the method, we plant fake movers in real data and count how many the search finds. In tests on 10 real fields, it recovers about 67% of the faint planted objects.

Benefits


One web page replaces several desktop programs and command-line steps.
It shows its own evidence: the originals sit beside the stack, and limits are stated when data is thin.
The search is tested, with a measured recovery rate instead of a claim.
It also overlays published Planet X sky regions, so users can see where proposals point and researchers have a good starting point on identifying those candidates.

What we hope to achieve


We want students, teachers, volunteers and researchers to explore real SPHEREx data without expert software. Next steps are live catalog cross-matching, reporting confirmed finds to the Minor Planet Center, and testing with real users.

Tools and technology


Data: NASA SPHEREx Level 2 images via NASA-IPAC IRSA.
Backend: Python, FastAPI, NumPy and Astropy, SQLite, It has an offline demo bundle.
Frontend: React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4.
